usage: Very common collocation; 사회 often pairs with an adjective-like noun in front.
Compound noun used constantly in news and writing.
social life / life in the working world
Note: this usually means working life and getting along with people, not 'social life' in the party sense.
to go out into society (e.g., after school)
Idiomatic for entering the workforce / adult world.
examples: 우리 사회에는 아직 해결해야 할 문제가 많아요.
There are still many problems our society needs to solve.
해결해야 할 = 'that must be solved'; 사회 takes 에 for 'in society'.
대학을 졸업하면 본격적으로 사회생활을 시작해요.
Once you graduate from university, you really start your working life.
사회생활 here = professional/adult life, a key nuance.
인터넷이 우리 사회를 크게 바꿔 놓았어요.
The internet has greatly changed our society.
바꿔 놓다 = 'has changed (and left it that way)', natural with 사회.
nuance: 사회 covers 'society' as the whole community of people, but in everyday Korean 사회생활 and 사회에 나가다 specifically point to working life and entering the adult world. When Koreans say someone is good at 사회생활, they mean that person handles workplace relationships and social obligations well, not that they go to many parties.
mistakes: Assuming 사회생활 means 'social life / hanging out with friends' — it almost always means working life and getting along at work.
Using 사회 for a small social gathering; for that use 모임 instead.

usage: 전통 is frequently used attributively before another noun without 의.
지키다 ('protect, keep') is the standard verb that goes with 전통.
The adjective form; e.g. 전통적인 결혼식 = a traditional wedding.
오랜 ('long, longtime') is the natural modifier, not 긴.
examples: 한국의 전통을 지키려고 노력하는 사람들이 많아요.
Many people are working to preserve Korea's traditions.
지키려고 노력하다 = 'try to preserve', a common pattern with 전통.
이 마을은 오래된 전통을 그대로 이어 가고 있어요.
This village is carrying on its old traditions just as they are.
이어 가다 = 'carry on / continue', natural with 전통.
저는 전통적인 음악보다 현대 음악을 더 좋아해요.
I like modern music more than traditional music.
전통적인 = adjective form modifying 음악.
nuance: 전통 refers to customs, values, or practices handed down over generations. Use the adjective 전통적이다 (전통적인 + noun) when you describe something as 'traditional'; 전통 by itself is the abstract noun. It carries a respectful, valued tone, unlike the more neutral 습관 ('habit'), which is personal and routine.
mistakes: Saying 긴 전통 for 'long tradition' — Koreans say 오랜 전통.
Confusing 전통 (tradition) with 습관 (personal habit); 전통 is shared and inherited, 습관 is individual.

usage: 현대 commonly modifies another noun directly: 현대 사회, 현대 미술, 현대 의학.
Adjective form; 현대적인 디자인 = a modern design.
현대 + 인 (person) = the people of today; very common in essays.
entering modern times; in the modern era
Set phrase for 'in modern times', often starting a sentence.
examples: 현대 사회에서는 스마트폰 없이 살기 어려워요.
In modern society it's hard to live without a smartphone.
현대 사회에서는 = 'in modern society', a frequent opener.
현대인은 늘 시간에 쫓기며 살아요.
People today live constantly chased by time.
현대인 = 'modern people'; 쫓기며 = 'being chased'.
이 건물은 전통과 현대가 잘 어우러져 있어요.
This building blends tradition and modernity well.
전통과 현대 is a common paired contrast; 어우러지다 = 'harmonize'.
nuance: 현대 means the modern/contemporary age and is usually used as a noun modifier (현대 사회, 현대 미술) rather than standing alone. For the descriptive sense 'modern, up-to-date in style', use the adjective 현대적이다. It is often contrasted with 전통 to set up old-versus-new comparisons.
mistakes: Using 현대 to mean 'recently' — for that use 최근 or 요즘.
Forgetting the adjective form: say 현대적인 디자인, not 현대 디자인, when you mean 'modern-style design'.

usage: 국가 is the formal word for a country as a political entity; 나라 is the everyday word.
국가 modifies many official nouns: 국가 정책, 국가 기관.
Formal, often heard about public service or soldiers.
국가적 + noun, e.g. 국가적 행사 = a national event.
examples: 국가는 국민의 안전을 책임져야 해요.
The state must take responsibility for its citizens' safety.
국가 paired with 국민; 책임지다 = 'take responsibility'.
이번 행사는 국가적인 차원에서 준비되고 있어요.
This event is being prepared on a national level.
국가적인 차원에서 = 'at a national level', a formal collocation.
여러 국가가 이 문제를 함께 논의했어요.
Several nations discussed this issue together.
여러 국가 = 'several nations'; 논의하다 = 'discuss (formally)'.
nuance: 국가 is the formal, institutional word for a country as a political and legal entity, used in news, law, and academic contexts. In casual speech, Koreans say 나라 instead (우리 나라, not usually 우리 국가). Choose 국가 when the emphasis is on government, policy, or the state as an institution.
mistakes: Saying 우리 국가 in casual conversation — the natural phrase is 우리 나라.
Treating 국가 and 나라 as fully interchangeable; 국가 is formal/institutional, 나라 is everyday.

usage: Extremely common in news; 정부 modifies the noun directly.
발표하다 is the standard verb for official government statements.
Often heard regarding funding, benefits, or aid.
examples: 정부가 새로운 부동산 정책을 발표했어요.
The government announced a new real estate policy.
정부 + 발표하다, the textbook news collocation.
많은 사람들이 정부의 결정에 반대하고 있어요.
Many people are opposing the government's decision.
정부의 결정 = 'the government's decision'; 반대하다 = 'oppose'.
정부에서 소상공인을 위한 지원을 늘리기로 했어요.
The government decided to increase support for small business owners.
정부에서 (subject marked with 에서 for organizations) is natural and common.
nuance: 정부 means the government as an administrative body. Note that when an organization is the subject of an action, Korean often marks it with 에서 (정부에서 발표했어요) as well as 가 (정부가 발표했어요); both are correct, with 에서 feeling slightly more institutional. Pair it with formal verbs like 발표하다, 결정하다, 지원하다.
mistakes: Confusing 정부 (the government/administration) with 정치 (politics, the activity); 정부 is the body, 정치 is the field.
Using only 가 as the subject marker; with organizations like 정부, the 에서 form (정부에서) is equally natural.

usage: 관심이 있다/없다 is the go-to phrase for topics like 정치.
정치 + 인; the person who does politics.
Adjective form; 정치적인 문제 = a political issue.
to go into / be in politics
하다 here means to be active in the political arena.
examples: 저는 정치에 별로 관심이 없어요.
I'm not very interested in politics.
정치에 관심이 없다, the standard way to talk about interest.
요즘 정치 뉴스를 보면 답답할 때가 많아요.
These days, watching political news often feels frustrating.
정치 뉴스 = 'political news'; 답답하다 = 'stifling, frustrating'.
그 문제는 너무 정치적이라서 이야기하기 조심스러워요.
That issue is too political, so I'm careful about discussing it.
정치적이라서 = 'because it's political', adjective + 라서.
nuance: 정치 is the abstract field of politics, while 정부 is the concrete governing body and 정치인 is an individual politician. The adjective 정치적이다 describes something as 'political' (often with an undertone of being calculated or sensitive). Koreans frequently treat 정치 as a touchy topic, so 정치적인 이야기 is something many avoid in polite company.
mistakes: Mixing up 정치 (politics) and 정부 (government) — politics is the activity/field, government is the institution.
Saying 정치 사람 for 'politician'; the correct word is 정치인 (or 정치가).

usage: 어렵다 (lit. 'difficult') is the idiomatic way to say the economy is in a slump.
Two senses: 'economical (cheap)' and 'economic/financial'. 경제적인 부담 = financial burden.
경제 takes modifiers like 세계, 한국, 지역 directly.
examples: 요즘 경제가 어려워서 다들 지갑을 닫고 있어요.
The economy is tough these days, so everyone is tightening their wallets.
경제가 어렵다 + 지갑을 닫다 ('close one's wallet') = natural idiomatic pairing.
정부는 경제 성장을 위해 여러 정책을 내놓았어요.
The government put forward various policies for economic growth.
경제 성장을 위해 = 'for economic growth'; 내놓다 = 'put forward'.
대중교통을 이용하는 게 훨씬 경제적이에요.
Using public transportation is much more economical.
경제적이다 here means 'economical/cost-saving', the everyday sense.
nuance: 경제 means 'economy' as a system, but the adjective 경제적이다 splits into two everyday meanings: 'economical' (saves money) and 'economic/financial' (경제적 부담 = financial burden). To say the economy is doing badly, Koreans say 경제가 어렵다 or 경제가 안 좋다 rather than translating 'bad' literally.
mistakes: Translating 'the economy is bad' word-for-word with 나쁘다 — natural Korean is 경제가 어렵다 or 경제가 안 좋다.
Forgetting that 경제적이다 can mean 'economical (saves money)', not only 'economic'.

usage: 제도 = an organized social system of rules; pairs with 교육, 의료, 복지.
바꾸다 ('change') and 고치다 ('fix') are common verbs with 제도.
도입하다 ('introduce, adopt') is the formal verb for bringing in a 제도.
examples: 한국의 의료 제도는 외국인들에게도 잘 되어 있어요.
Korea's healthcare system is well set up even for foreigners.
의료 제도 = 'medical system'; 잘 되어 있다 = 'is well established'.
회사가 재택근무 제도를 새로 도입했어요.
The company newly introduced a work-from-home system.
제도 + 도입하다, the standard collocation for adopting a system.
이건 한 사람의 잘못이 아니라 제도적인 문제예요.
This isn't one person's fault but a systemic problem.
제도적인 문제 = 'systemic/structural problem', a useful set phrase.
nuance: 제도 refers to an established system of rules or an institution in the abstract sense — an education system, a welfare system, a company policy framework. It is more structural than 법률 (specific laws) and more formal than 규칙 ('rules' for daily situations). The adjective 제도적이다 is handy for saying a problem is 'systemic' rather than individual.
mistakes: Confusing 제도 (a system/framework of rules) with 규칙 (everyday rules); 제도 is large-scale and institutional.
Using 제도 for a physical institution/building — for a building use 기관 or the specific place name.

usage: 지키다 ('keep, observe') is the standard verb; cf. 법을 어기다 = break the law.
법률 modifies formal nouns: 법률 상담, 법률 문제, 법률 전문가.
제정하다 is the formal verb for legislating; very written/news register.
examples: 새로운 법률이 다음 달부터 시행돼요.
A new law goes into effect starting next month.
법률 + 시행되다 ('be enforced/take effect'), formal collocation.
이 문제는 법률 전문가의 도움이 필요해요.
This issue needs help from a legal expert.
법률 전문가 = 'legal expert'; 도움이 필요하다 = 'need help'.
모든 국민은 법률 앞에서 평등해요.
All citizens are equal before the law.
법률 앞에서 평등하다 = 'equal before the law', a formal set expression.
nuance: 법률 is the formal, written term for 'law' (as in legislation and the legal system), common in documents, news, and academic contexts. In everyday speech, Koreans usually shorten it to 법 (법을 어기다 = break the law). Use 법률 when the register is official or when referring to laws as a body of legislation; use 법 in casual conversation.
mistakes: Using 법률 in casual speech where 법 is natural — say 법을 어기다, not 법률을 어기다, when chatting.
Confusing 법률 (the law itself) with 법원 (the court); 법원 is the institution that applies the law.

usage: 잡다 ('grab') is the idiomatic verb for gaining political power.
남용하다 ('misuse, abuse') is a frequent and important pairing.
권력 + 자 (person); someone who holds authority.
다툼 ('struggle, fight') captures conflict over authority.
examples: 권력을 가진 사람일수록 더 책임감을 가져야 해요.
The more power a person has, the more responsibility they should bear.
권력을 가지다 + V-(으)ㄹ수록 ('the more...'), a strong intermediate combo.
그 정치인은 권력을 남용해서 결국 자리에서 물러났어요.
That politician abused his power and eventually stepped down.
권력을 남용하다 + 물러나다 ('step down'), natural news-style phrasing.
역사를 보면 권력은 영원하지 않아요.
Looking at history, power is not eternal.
권력은 영원하지 않다 = 'power is not eternal', a reflective set sentence.
nuance: 권력 specifically means political power or authority — the power to control people and decisions — and carries a weightier, often serious or negative tone (권력 남용 = abuse of power). It is different from 힘, which is general 'strength/power' (physical, emotional, or influence) used in everyday life. Reserve 권력 for the political/institutional sense.
mistakes: Using 권력 for physical strength or everyday 'power' — for those use 힘.
Saying 권력을 하다; power is something you 잡다 (seize), 가지다 (have), or 행사하다 (exercise), not 하다.

english: the people; citizens of a nation
usage: 국민 pairs with 권리 ('rights') and 의무 ('duties') in civic contexts.
전 ('whole') + 국민 = everyone in the country.
Fixed compound; a vote by all citizens.
뽑다 ('choose, elect') is the natural verb in election contexts.
examples: 국가는 국민의 안전과 행복을 위해 일해야 해요.
The state should work for the safety and happiness of its citizens.
국가 + 국민, the classic civic pairing.
이 정책은 전 국민에게 영향을 줘요.
This policy affects all citizens.
전 국민 = 'all citizens'; 영향을 주다 = 'have an effect on'.
국민이 직접 대통령을 뽑아요.
The people directly elect the president.
국민이 뽑다 = 'the people elect', simple civic sentence.
nuance: 국민 means the people as citizens of a particular nation — a civic, collective term tied to rights, duties, and the state. It differs from 사람들 ('people' in general) and 시민 ('citizens', which leans toward city residents or civil society). Use 국민 when talking about the population in relation to government, law, or national identity.
mistakes: Using 국민 to mean 'people' in a casual, general sense — for that use 사람들.
Confusing 국민 (citizens of a nation) with 시민 (citizens in the civil-society / city-resident sense).
